title: How sites tell people from bots | Blog Example

How sites tell people from bots
Blog Example | Security notes | 12 March 2026
Most of us meet a bot check a few times a week and barely notice it. A page says "Just a moment" or "Checking if the site connection is secure", a spinner turns for a second or two, and the real page appears. Behind that pause the site is asking one question: is this a person in a normal browser, or a script hammering the server?
The quiet checks
The cheapest checks are invisible. The site looks at how the browser connects, whether cookies and JavaScript work, and how fast the requests come. A normal visit passes without a single click. When the signals look odd, the site asks for more.
The visible checks
The next step is a box that says "Verify you are human", sometimes with a checkbox, sometimes with a puzzle. Some sites ask you to press and hold a button until it fills up. Others show a grid of photos and ask you to pick every bus or every traffic light. Each of these costs a real person a few seconds and costs a script a great deal more.
Codes are a different thing
Bot checks are not the same as sign-in checks. When a bank sends a verification code to your phone, it already knows who you claim to be and wants proof that you hold the phone. That is two-factor sign-in, and it protects your account rather than the site's servers.
What this means for you
If a check appears on every visit, try another network, clear the site's cookies, or update your browser. If a page keeps asking you to verify you are human after you have passed, the site may be blocking your whole network for a while. Waiting a few minutes usually helps, and so does writing to the site's support team with the time of the visit.
